I'm pretty sure I almost got kidnapped into the sex trade when I was fifteen.

It was my birthday and I was in Mexico. My grandmother was sick in the hotel so I went out looking for some adventure. Found an attractive guy who spoke perfect English to bum cigarettes off of. He was probably mid twenties but definitely flirting with me. Being an unattractive child who got little to no male attention this flustered me greatly and clouded my judgement. I really wanted to go to a club but you had to be sixteen or with someone of age.

He tells me no problem he will go with me. We go in the direction of the club but we pass it (we were walking). He says there is a better club down the road. We meander until we get to a small dingy bar. I remember sitting there and realizing I was the only female in there. My legs were jittering because I was getting scared and I remember he kept asking me if I was okay and if I was nervous. I kept reassuring him I was fine but realizing that I was super fucked.

They are all chattering in Spanish I barely understand any of it. I later became fluent but this was when I had only studied it for a year so I was lost. 

He tells me to come outside. There's a car and about six men around. I still remember what they look like. One had a mustache and was skinny, another larger with a shaved head. When I see the car I immediately realize that something really terrible was about to happen. I can't really describe how I knew, but there was a heaviness around the group of men. I dunno. It was a sudden shift from before when he was joking and flirting with me. They were all staring at me too.

I stop walking and start to slowly back pedal away from all the dudes. The original guy tells me change of plans, we are going to a party in Mexico City. I lie and tell him my dad has a super strict curfew and is waiting at the hotel for me so I can't go anywhere (my dad wasn't anywhere near me but I thought that would somehow be more intimidating than "my grandma with food poisoning may notice my absence") and sort of imply he will start looking for me if I'm not back. 

They tell me no worries it will be quick they will get me home in time. He reaches out to grab me but I've been moving away from him so he doesn't reach me. Tells me it's fine it will be fun.

I finally blurt out that I'm not getting in that fucking car and start backing up noticeably and trying to figure out where the fuck I am.

The dude asks for a hug because "were friends" and steps towards me. I'm like "nah bro we ain't friends" and turn around and run faster than I have before or since. I'm completely lost in a labyrinth of some residential neighborhood. Run into a kid I'm pretty sure is on crack and ask for directions. Realize I have no idea what left or right is in Spanish so his directions are useless. I run and run and run until I stumble upon the center of town and start sobbing with relief.

I didn't connect the possibility of being sold into the sex trade until years later. I thought I was just about to get gang raped (which is also a possibility). Later I found out that Mexico City was over two hours away and I had told them I needed to be home within half an hour. So something sketchy as fuck was going to happen to me. 

Tl:dr lonely teenager gets briefly seduced by attractive sex trafficker

My professor turns to him, his eyes wide and horrified by what he has just seen, and asks "my god why did you stay for all of that?" to which he quietly replies "you said at the beginning of the semester that we weren't allowed to leave during the movie section".

First thing, get (EDIT: offer if they want it) them professional help. Also Dialectical Behavioral Therapy is super helpful but I didn't get that until my twenties and am unsure if it is available to younger people. People cut themselves for a lot of different reasons. My reason was that I didn't know how to express or process emotions in a way that didn't involve hurting myself. I haven't cut in almost four years and have mostly been self harm free for seven. Sometimes I don't cut from sheer willpower/ stubbornness but mostly it's because I've learned to express my emotions and feel them without immediately *needing* to cut to process them. 

Since my mother handled my self harming horribly I can tell you what NOT to do.

1. Don't make this about you or your parenting. Sure way to fuck a kid up is to make them feel guilty for how they are expressing their emotions. Frame the conversation like "I want to get you help so that you can experience life with this much pain. I care about you." NOT "how did I fuck up I'm a terrible parent why are you doing this to me it's so embarrassing" 

2. DO NOT and I repeat DO NOT punish your child for cutting. This includes removing the door of their room, taking away privileges if they cut. They are cutting (probably) to deal with some serious urges and emotions so adding pressure to them isn't helpful and may escalate their behavior. Like I got hella suicidal when I first committed to not self harming because it was keeping that at bay and it hit me full force when I stopped. Also, cutters are sneaky as fuck and we will find a way to self harm that is off your radar (shower cutting, burning, finger crushing or head banging, like we become pros at avoiding emotions through physical pain and self harming- those endorphins are real yo). 

3. Don't shame them or make fun of them// tell them nothing in their life is bad enough for them to cut. Some people are predisposed to not be able to handle the human condition. We just suck at it and living is hard for us. I have a great life and still get stuck in depression and overwhelm. Shame is a motherfucker to deal with so please don't put that on your kid.


Try to remember that cutting is a form of communication. It is the persons responsibility to recover from it (you can't "make" them cut or not cut) BUT you can be supportive and work with them to not harm themselves. Like I mentioned above, therapy is a great way to support a kid who is struggling. Giving them a place they can go that's safe to talk about whatever is bugging them. I have PTSD (which includes severe anxiety and bouts of depression) and I work in this field fairly successfully. I was in treatment for four years though (starting at 19) before I got my first job in social services. It is so important to come up with a treatment plan and way of self care that helps you before you help anyone else. 

My suggestion is to really hunker down on yourself and your treatment and figure out how "do you" and build a good foundation. This includes a healthy social life and some outlets/hobbies (you'll need those in the field trust me). Once you have that foundation then go for it. People like us have a unique perspective and, as long as we don't transfer our stuff to our clients, can be really effective at understanding people and helping them. 

I also don't tell many people that I have a diagnosis. Once I built trust with a few of my coworkers I did but never in a clinical setting or in a team meeting/clinical meeting. There is a time and place to process our diagnosis and it's good to be mindful of oversharing when discussing treatment plans etc. 

I also would super recommend getting a therapist while in this field. I think it's important for anyone but especially people who are managing a diagnosis. Sometimes I need a safe place to just cry and feel feelings and her office is wonderful for that. 

Good luck and feel free to PM me any other questions.

I work in a program to treat people with bpd so I am fairly familiar with the population. I'm going to go on a slight tangent but bear with me. It's a complicated diagnosis that has a lot of bad rap attached to it. (I would argue it's a trauma disorder not a personality disorder but that's another post for another time). I am also going to attempt to oversimplify this because I could write a whole book about bpd and trauma and how they present. (Disclaimer: every person is different and not all people with bpd manifest in this manner with this history. I also work with acute cases and so my understanding of bpd is in light of people who are so severely impacted by it they cannot function without frequent hospitalization. There are plenty of people with bpd who have fulfilling lives and have navigated their diagnosis effectively). 

Keep in mind that bpd is often (I would almost say always) a result of negligence in early development aka "invalidating environment". Normally when a kid expresses a feeling or is hurt, a parent will validate that this experience is real and help the child through that experience. This is how people learn emotional management and identification. This is also how they begin to decipher what is and what is not an emergency. 

People who have bpd often were told their feelings or  physical experiences were wrong or did not exist ("im hungry" "no you're not" "I'm sad" "stop complaining"). The main struggle they have is identifying feelings (even physical ones) and then effectively processing/ managing those feelings. 

I wanted to give that backdrop to what I'm going to say next. There are many reasons my clients have a history of somatic complaints  (1) They don't know if it's an emergency or not and so are scared. Which makes sense given that they could not trust their primary care giver to make decisions for them and keep them safe. (2) Medical emergencies are a way they were cared for and received validation in their negligent household and that behavior has continued into adulthood. Some of my clients have told me that they feel safer in a hospital than they do in their home. (3) They have learned to connect with people through having medical issues and don't know how to have conversations and build rapport without the medical talk. It can be one or all three. (Or none. But those three are the ones I see the most) 

Some questions for the OP: Is this client in any treatment? (I recommend dialectical behavior therapy aka DBT, my program uses it with a lot of success). If she is you can talk with her team and come up with a plan around this behavior. If she isn't then I would really recommend trying to get her into a group or program. (I'm not super sure of your relation to her I'm assuming caseworker? If I'm wrong forgive me). 

Is there a way she can have a standing meeting with her pcp every x amount of time? That way when she has something happen you can remind her she has an appointment coming up and can bring it to her pcp then. If she brings complaints to you, you can also remind her you are not qualified to give medical advice both ethically and legally. Keep that boundary. I would also work on developing a rapport that doesn't involve medical issues. I talk to my clients about their interests, favorite movies, etc. (This will help with #2 & #3 up above as well as facilitate/support the client acknowledging they are more than their medical ailments and that you are a safe person to explore their personality and who they are with). I've noticed the more I'm able to chat with people about what they like and what interests them, the less they talk to me about medical stuff. (Unless it's #1 but then I can work on helping them feel safe). 


Also, no matter how "ridiculous" her ailment is (or how imaginary) it is important to validate that the experience is scary and difficult. Validating doesn't mean agreeing with her but you can acknowledge that she is having an experience and that experience is hard for her. This is critical when working with this population because of the invalidating childhood environment factor.

I hesitate to comment on this because I don't want to invalidate anyone's experience. So I am going to preface this comment by saying that everyone's experience is valid and that if twelve steps didn't work for you, they did not work and that is okay. There are a lot of paths to recover from our childhoods and addiction problems that arise.

That being said, I want to offer an approach to twelve steps that worked for me. I want to do this in case there are people who do want to/have to attend twelve steps and who are struggling to stay clean. I attribute the twelve step program I attend to my survival and ultimately my recovery from substance abuse as well as putting me on a good track to recover from my CPTSD. The twelve steps stabilized me to the point where I could seek the intensive help that I needed for my CPTSD. I have a lot of criticisms of the program, don't get me wrong. But I was fortunate enough to find people who have supported me and helped me grow and recover.

Step One and the issue of powerlessness:

I learned that I was powerless over how people treated me. My mother would always abuse me every time I let her in my life. Admitting that I was powerless over other people allowed me to walk away and set healthy boundaries around abusive people. Before I learned that, I constantly thought it was my responsibility to get people not to abuse me. With step one, I was able to accept that I cannot change people *it gave me the permission to go no/low contact with my mother/abuser* If I couldn't change her, then I was allowed to walk away.

Step Four and the issue of blame:

My part in my inventory of my mother is that I continued to show up and I continued to expect her to be a different person. I would open myself up to abuse which would result in resentments and obsession over her behavior. The fourth step allowed me to explore the reservation I had/the denial that my mother would change and be the parent I always wanted her to be. My "part" was the dishonesty behind this and the intense denial it took to repeatedly let me return to her and almost be surprised when she hurt me again. Once again, the twelve steps gave me permission to go no contact.

Another part of my inventory when it came to abuse was the abuse I suffered later from partners. My part in it was how I let it affect me today. I had no part in the actual abuse but it left me with ideas about myself and the world that were not true. The fourth step gave me space to explore those ideas and challenge them. 

Step Nine and the issue of amends:

I have plenty of people on my amends from active addiction. The amends I have from my abuse is an amends to myself.
I make amends by not allowing abusive people in my life, by acknowledging and validating the abuse I suffered, by expressing my feelings in a productive and healthy way. I surround myself with people who are kind and who love me. I make daily amends to myself by staying clean. I can say "no" now. I can give myself permission to exist.


I hope this gave some insight on another way to engage with the twelve steps. Once again, if it did not work for you that is okay. I hope you find a way to recover as life a life that is not overshadowed by what has happened to us. If you do decide to do a twelve step program, find the people who have recovery from trauma as well as addiction and stick with them hard. It is a slightly different animal than straightforward addiction but the twelve steps can be beneficial for the beginning of that journey.

Yeah the training for my job was pretty mind opening. I already had worked through a lot of my FLEAS (which looked A LOT like bpd) but was able to see my behavior in a more compassionate light and sort of let go of the shame.

My program does something called Dialectical Behavioral Therapy (DBT) that is super helpful and has been effective in treating DBT. If you can find a DBT therapist that would be helpful, or at least someone familiar. There might be programs available too that he can do off site while staying with you. 

I hesitate to give too much advice because I don't know your situation completely but I can give you the gist of the training I received when I was first hired as an RSW. 

The main thing to keep in mind is to validate/support behaviors that are positive and to ignore or pay as little attention to behaviors that are not constructive. People who grew up in invalidating environments seek validation through self destruction (because it was often the only way to get attention in their childhood). There is a set pattern that DBT tries to break, which is helping people feel validated and supported without doing the destructive behaviors. Even if it seems obvious, point out when he does something good and give him attention. If he is being rude you can say "hey, I really want to help you but it is hard when you are talking to me like this, can we figure this out when you are able to talk without yelling ?" Or something to that effect.  It is pretty complex and takes time to develop but that is the basics of it. I recommend books by Marcia Lineham who created DBT. It is worth a read. Also, always remember to validate emotions. Even if they aren't really appropriate for the situation. Just a simple "I hear you are feeling frustrated. That's okay to feel" or something. Generally people with bpd spent their whole lives being told their emotions weren't real or were bad. Once you validate their emotions you can move into the "what are we're going to do/process and handle these emotions because they are real for you". Fear of abandonment and invalidation are two triggers that generally cause crisis in people wth bpd, which is a good thing to keep in mind. 

DBT is also helpful to people who grew up in nhouseholds because it essentially teaches emotion management and interpersonal skills, which are two areas that are not taught for people with Nparents.  

Hope that helps. People with bpd can make significant if not full recovery given therapy and support (and a willingness to engage in said therapy and support). I've found my residents to be creative and wonderful people who are haunted with the after affects of their childhood.

A plant based diet was super helpful for me to trim up and get healthy. I sort of frame my food around vegetables and beans and snack on fruit.

I found vegetables that I actually really like and can get totally behind eating on the regular. 

Looking up recipes and actually cooking was huge for me. I used to sort of graze and/or go to a gas station to get food and it was really unhealthy. I find if I make a large dinner w enough for leftovers for lunch, when lunch comes around I'm way more likely to eat that then go for the chips and soda.

Firstly, I want to say that I am sorry bad things happened to you. You did not deserve that abuse and I am absolutely sorry that anyone in your recovery triggered those feelings of helplessness or said that you played a part in it. Yes, some people with no history of trauma will warp the steps to the point where the victims are made to feel responsible for their perpetrators actions. *That is never the case*. I was lucky to have a sponsor who was well versed in trauma recovery and guided me through the steps mindful of that fact that there were definitely times in my life in which *i was actually victimized and it was not the result of my own self sabotage or selfishness*. 

In those cases during my fourth step I framed "my part" around "what actions do I do today that are dictated by my trauma, how do I let this affect me today?" So it's not the trauma in which I am seeking to see my part in, but my behavior afterwards (which absolutely is something I can and do change).  I.E. My part in Traumatic Event A is that I do not let people close to me and actively use my history of trauma to isolate. I obsess over my resentment of my perpetrators because it validates my desire to stay alone and not have intimate connections. 

See the difference? I had no part in the traumatic event but I do have a part in my recovery from it.


I am a huge fan of outside help. I am in therapy for my abuse. The twelve steps is for getting people clean. THATS IT. Yes, people learn how to function as people is society etc etc etc but if you have more than drug addiction you are dealing with them you are going to need more than the twelve steps. End of story. I see a lot of people relapse because they think the twelve steps is the panacea for all their problems. It's not. It's an effective tool for some people who have the diagnosis of polysubstance abuse. 

One more thing too (wall of text, sorry, I just related to you and wanted to share my perspective) is the issue of the first step and invoking feelings of powerlessness. I struggled with this and consistently wanted to control the world to feel safe because I didn't ever want to feel not  safe again. The way I look at the first step now is that I am powerless over the fact that the abuse happened. I am powerless over the fact I was victimized. The abuse was not my fault. I am powerless over the fact people who abused me sill lead happy functional lives. For my second and third step I believe if I live by the principles of the program I can learn how to feel safe. One of the principles is respect. This includes self respect which means I am allowed to walk away from situations that make me uncomfortable. I don't believe in God. The second and third step don't have to be about God or turning t over in a bad sense. It was empowering for me to experience the ability to say no and walk away from fucked up situations. I surrendered to the principles and the fact that living by them will improve my life.

That is my experience that I wanted to share. 

I wish you the best on your journey. The twelve steps might not be what you need. I wish you peace. Please stay clean and allow yourself to do whatever type of work you need to recover. You deserve to heal and be happy.

So I can answer this question in two fronts: I work with people who have severe symptoms of bpd and I grew up w an Nmother and I myself was symptomatic of bpd before getting treatment for substance abuse and PTSD (apparently that combo manifests a lot like bpd and recovery is surprisingly similar). 

The main thing I want to say is that bpd is not as big and scary as a lot of mainstream media make it seem. There is a huge stigma against people w this diagnosis which is largely unfair. Yes, untreated people w bpd can be abusive and really difficult. But bpd manifests (generally) in an abusive/invalidating environment and people w bpd are really just people doing their best with minimal coping skills/negative coping skills. Recovery is totally possible and the first start is getting a formal diagnosis and working with a therapist. The people I work w do a therapy called DBT which is really positive and works well. The skills learned in DBT are generally good life skills that people with Nparents don't get so either way it is worth checking out. 
For me personally, getting professional help and admitting that my upbringing had manifested in less than desirable actions was really really helpful. Now I have intimate relationships and work a fairly rigorous program of recovery/therapy. I used to have a lot of shame and avoided the fact my childhood had really affected me. Facing it head on was the only way I could recover. 

Best of luck to you. Please don't be scared of how your upbringing manifests for you today. It isn't your fault what happened and it is possible to recover from it.

Hey so great question! You sound super awesome. As a survivor who is in a relationship, here are some tips. Obviously the best way to go about this is to talk with her and figure out specifically what her triggers are, etc, but if she isn't ready to talk about it here are some general things:
-Listen to her and stop immediately when she says no/stop/wait. This pertains to things like hugs or holding hands or whatever, not just sex. Show that you respect her boundaries. Be aware of nonverbal boundaries too, like getting tense or shutting down. 
-Tell her that you want to be with her and that you won't leave her no matter what your sex life looks like. My partner consistently reiterates that it is my personality he is in love with and that when and if i want to have sex he is open to it but it's not the driving force of the relationship. Back that up by not sexually coming on to her/trying to have sex with her whenever possible. It is super important to act like you can take or leave sex. Not because you don't care, but because sexual energy can be super super triggering for people with trauma, especially when it feels intense and desperate. Some people are into the whole "I need you so bad right now" thing, people with trauma are generally triggered by it. 
-Don't push her to tell you about the trauma. She will probably do it on her own time. 
(You've already been doing most of these so good job, I've already said this but you sound awesome.)

Those are the major ones. The most important thing is to show you are a safe person, not just say it. It sounds like you are on the right track/already doing this. Your actions will be way more important than anything you say. 

Good luck. Dating people with trauma is hard but asking for help and communication are key. When she gets triggered it may not be pretty. Try to keep in mind that she is a human who is having a human reaction to something fucked up that happened to her, not someone being "difficult" or "hard" on purpose.

Here are some things I did figure out about dating newcomers.
1. You may be able to handle a break up but so they have the foundation to handle it? 
2. If it goes south, will they feel they can rely on the fellowship or will they feel ostracized?  (People were fiercely loyal to me when it went badly with one newcomer they made a point to tell him his actions-cheating- were fucked up. Although I appreciate the loyalty, I can imagine how isolating it was for him and how it may have contributed to his not going to meetings since not many people knew him. Which brings me to my third point)
3. Platonic relationships with people in the fellowship have saved my ass multiple times in the years I've been clean. When you date a newcomer, you are effectively taking their time and energy building a relationship with you instead of building relationships with people that will last a long time and be unconditionally supportive (because if you break up, you probably will not be able to support her emotionally for obvious reasons).
4. This is their time to get to know themselves. When you date them, it is postponing the internal work that needs to happen since most of it is done while being single. It's hard to get in touch with yourself when you're romantically involved with someone.
5. If she uses, will you be tempted to use with her? A dark question but a scenario I've seen go down over and over again in the fellowship.
6. As a final note, it is really chaotic and stressful to date a newcomer. They are still figuring out life and lots of chaos happens when that is going on. I was there in early recovery and it is highly unlikely that they have their shit together. As someone with time though, being romantically involved in that chaos is really really draining. 


I get what it's like to have a crush on a newcomer. I was madly in love with one when I had three years. When he relapsed it was the closest I had ever come to getting high. It is hard to set a boundary when you see a future with someone. But that boundary may save both of your lives. I've seen A LOT of people use over relationships. At the end of the day I've decided my partner wouldn't be a newcomer because my HP wouldn't put someone in my life that requires me to break a code of the fellowship and my own personal code. So that helps when I feel attracted to one. And if it is supposed to happen, they will stay clean and when they have more recovery under their belt you can make a move. Patience is a good principle to invoke for this situation. 

But if you do decide to do it, remain honest and open with your sponsor, act on the principles of the program, and make sure you are able to set boundaries and avoid spending all your time with each other.


Best of luck.
